_**User (2026-11-07 21:11:28Z)**_

Add Configurable Low-Stock Thresholds and Warnings #61

User Story
As a store manager, I want to configure low-stock thresholds for inventory items so that I can identify products that need to be restocked before they sell out.

User Scenario
A store manager is reviewing inventory in the Medusa admin dashboard. They select an inventory item and set its low-stock threshold to 10 units. Later, when the available quantity falls to 8 units, the inventory list displays a "Low Stock" warning for that item. If the quantity reaches 0, the item is marked "Out of Stock." The manager can update the threshold as inventory needs change.

Acceptance Criteria
Store managers can configure and update a non-negative integer low-stock threshold for an inventory item through the admin interface.
Threshold values are persisted and remain unchanged after refreshing the page.
Inventory items display a "Low Stock" warning when their available quantity is greater than 0 and less than or equal to their configured threshold.
Inventory items with an available quantity of 0 or less are labeled "Out of Stock," regardless of their configured threshold.
Items with available quantities above their configured threshold do not display a low-stock warning.
Existing inventory management functionality continues to work without modification.
Automated tests verify threshold validation, persistence, and stock-status classification.
Out of Scope
Email, SMS, or push notifications about low stock.
Automatic inventory replenishment or purchase orders.
A centralized inventory alerts dashboard (covered in a separate issue).
Historical tracking of inventory changes.
Open Questions
Should thresholds be configured per inventory item or per inventory item at each stock location?
Should items without a configured threshold use a default value, or should low-stock monitoring be disabled for those items?
How should inventory items that do not track stock be handled?

This is an issue I am going to start working on. Can you review the spec to make sure it is clear enough to implement and that it fits into the code?

```text
import {
  BigNumber,
  isDefined,
  MathBN,
  toMikroORMEntity,
} from "@medusajs/framework/utils"
import { Formula, OnInit } from "@medusajs/framework/mikro-orm/core"

import InventoryItem from "../models/inventory-item"
import InventoryLevel from "../models/inventory-level"

function applyHook() {
  const MikroORMEntity = toMikroORMEntity(InventoryLevel)

  MikroORMEntity.prototype["onInit"] = function () {
    if (isDefined(this.stocked_quantity) && isDefined(this.reserved_quantity)) {
      this.available_quantity = new BigNumber(
        MathBN.sub(this.raw_stocked_quantity, this.raw_reserved_quantity)
      )
    }
  }

  OnInit()(MikroORMEntity.prototype, "onInit")
}

function applyFormulas() {
  const MikroORMEntity = toMikroORMEntity(InventoryItem)

  Formula(
    (item) =>
      `(SELECT SUM(reserved_quantity) FROM inventory_level il WHERE il.inventory_item_id = ${item}.id AND il.deleted_at IS NULL)`,
    { lazy: true, serializer: Number, hidden: true, type: "number" }
  )(MikroORMEntity.prototype, "reserved_quantity")

  Formula(
    (item) =>
      `(SELECT SUM(stocked_quantity) FROM inventory_level il WHERE il.inventory_item_id = ${item}.id AND il.deleted_at IS NULL)`,
    { lazy: true, serializer: Number, hidden: true, type: "number" }
  )(MikroORMEntity.prototype, "stocked_quantity")
}
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-07 21:12:31Z)**_

The spec is mostly implementable, but there's one real blocker: a low-stock badge already exists in the code, and the spec doesn't mention it. Two of the three open questions need answers before you start. The third mostly goes away once you see how the code is set up.

## Blocker: there is already a low-stock badge

Issue #18 (commit `7fe156c453`) added a "Low stock" badge to the inventory list ([use-inventory-table-columns.tsx:93-113](packages/admin/dashboard/src/routes/inventory/inventory-list/components/use-inventory-table-columns.tsx#L93-L113)). It conflicts with this spec in four ways:

| Current behavior | What #61 says |
|---|---|
| The threshold is fixed at `< 10` | Each item has its own threshold, `<=` |
| It checks `stocked_quantity` | It checks **available** quantity |
| It shows "Low stock" at 0 | 0 or less shows "Out of Stock" |
| The label is plain English text | (not specified; the rest of the dashboard uses i18n keys) |

Its test ([use-inventory-table-columns.spec.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/routes/inventory/inventory-list/components/use-inventory-table-columns.spec.tsx)) checks a copy of the logic written inside the test file, not the real column, so it would keep passing whatever you change.

So the criterion "Existing inventory management functionality continues to work without modification" can't hold as written. #61 has to replace the #18 badge. The spec should say so, and that criterion should be reworded to something like "stock levels, reservations and location management are unaffected."

## Gaps in the spec

**1. "Available quantity" is not defined at the item level.**
- In the code, `available_quantity` only exists on each location level (stocked minus reserved, set in [apply-decorators.ts](packages/modules/inventory/src/utils/apply-decorators.ts)).
- The item itself only has `stocked_quantity` and `reserved_quantity`, each summed across locations.
- The spec should say: available = total stocked − total reserved, across all locations, with incoming quantity excluded.
- It should also say what happens to an item with **no location levels**. The sums come back null, so the item could be "Out of Stock" or have no status.

**2. Open Q1: per item or per location.** I'd recommend **per item**:
- The list shows one row per item with summed quantities, so a per-item threshold matches what the user sees.
- It's one nullable column on `InventoryItem`.
- Per location would mean a column on `InventoryLevel`, plus the status would live in the location-levels table on the detail page instead of the list. That's a bigger change, and it could be a follow-up issue.

**3. Open Q2: what an unset threshold means.** This also decides what happens to the #18 behavior. Two options:
- **Null means no low-stock warning, but "Out of Stock" still shows.** I'd recommend this. It's simple, and it matches the criterion that says out-of-stock applies regardless of threshold.
- **Default to 10.** This keeps the current #18 behavior for existing items.

Either is fine, but it has to be written down. Also state that a threshold of 0 means the item is never "Low Stock", which follows from the "> 0 and ≤ threshold" rule.

**4. Open Q3: items that don't track stock.** This mostly doesn't apply. Inventory items have no "track stock" flag; `manage_inventory` is on `ProductVariant` in the product module. As far as I know, variants with `manage_inventory = false` don't normally get an inventory item at all, so they never show up in the inventory list. I'd answer "out of scope: inventory items always track stock" rather than build anything for it.

**5. Where the status appears.** The scenario only mentions the inventory list. Say whether the detail page or product variant pages should show it too. Also say there is **no filtering or sorting by status**. The item-level quantities are lazy SQL sums, so a "show only low stock" filter would need real backend work.

## How it fits the code

This touches the full stack, which is bigger than it looks:

- **Module:** add `low_stock_threshold: model.number().nullable()` to [inventory-item.ts](packages/modules/inventory/src/models/inventory-item.ts), plus a migration. Use a real column rather than `metadata`, so the API can validate it.
- **Types:** `InventoryItemDTO`, the create/update DTOs, and the HTTP `AdminInventoryItem` in `packages/core/types`.
- **API:**
  - Add `z.number().int().min(0).nullish()` to the create/update validators in [validators.ts](packages/medusa/src/api/admin/inventory-items/validators.ts). This is where the "non-negative integer" rule gets enforced.
  - Add the field to `defaultAdminInventoryItemFields` in [query-config.ts](packages/medusa/src/api/admin/inventory-items/query-config.ts).
  - Decide whether the CSV import route (`inventory-items/import`) accepts it; I'd say no for now.
- **Dashboard:**
  - A threshold input in `inventory-detail/components/edit-inventory-item`.
  - Replace the #18 badge, using i18n keys for the labels.
  - Put the rule in a pure `getStockStatus(available, threshold)` function so Vitest tests the real logic.
- **Tests:**
  - Unit tests for `getStockStatus` (boundaries: −1, 0, threshold, threshold + 1, null threshold).
  - An HTTP integration test under `integration-tests/http/__tests__/` for validation (negative and decimal values rejected) and for the value persisting.

Once you settle Q1 and Q2, I can save the decisions to memory for the PR's design-decisions section, as with the earlier issues, or draft the open questions as a comment for the issue author.

```text
- Invalid value (negative, non-number, non-integer) throws at startup in the loader: `MedusaError` `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, as auth/payment/tax loaders do for bad module options.

Decided by the user (2026-10-28): leave the Redis engine's `ModuleOptions` declaration as is. It types `options` as the flat `RedisWorkflowsOptions`, but runtime and docs use `options.redis`, so it is already wrong. Later (2026-10-28) the user said to do only what the issue asks, so no new in-memory `ModuleOptions` declaration either; no type changes in #67. List the Redis mismatch under Tech Debt (encountered) in the PR.

Found while testing (2026-10-28): `deleteFromDb` deletes by `run_id`, and child runs share the parent's `runId`, so deleting a parent also deletes its children. The child-branch change in save() only shows when the parent is kept by its own `retentionTime` and the child isn't; the test for it uses that setup. Put in the PR under Tech Debt (encountered).

**Why:** Agreed before implementation; list in the PR description per [[pr-description-format]].
**How to apply:** The 0 case needs a change to the child-workflow branch of save() in both engines, not only the retention value; test it.
```

Review a change like the senior developer who will be paged when it breaks.
Order of importance: correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean.
Lean still matters: every extra line must be read, tested and fixed later.
This is a report the user asked for, so give it in full.

## 1. Understand first

- Review what the user names: uncommitted or staged changes, a branch, a PR
  link, or files. Nothing named: the uncommitted changes, or the last commit
  if there are none.
- Read the diff, then the code it touches: callers of every changed function,
  the functions it calls, the tests, the README.
- Trace the real flow: where data comes in, what is stored, what goes out.
- A change can break code it does not touch. When a signature, return value
  or behavior changes, grep every caller.
- Find the expected load in the repo (README, deploy config): one person
  running a script, or many users and processes at once. Judge scale against
  that, and say which load you assumed.

## 2. Look for

1. **Bug:** wrong result, crash, missed edge case (empty, zero, last item,
   rounding, time zones), a caller broken by the change, a fix applied in one
   caller while the shared function stays broken.
2. **Risk:** security holes (injection, weak randomness, secrets, missing
   checks on input from users), data loss (errors swallowed, writes in the
   wrong order, no transaction).
3. **Scale:** fine for one user, wrong for many: check-then-write races, the
   same work done by every process, memory or lists that only grow, a query
   per item, O(n^2) on big input, per-process state that must be shared.
4. **Missing test:** risky new logic (a branch, a parser, money, security,
   data writes, a bug fix) with no test that fails when it breaks. One good
   test, not coverage.
5. **Speed:** big slowdowns are problems. Small wins (work repeated in a hot
   loop) are suggestions; some software counts every millisecond.
6. **Lean:** code that should not exist or should be smaller.
   - delete: dead code, unused options, speculative features
   - reuse: the repo already has this helper (name the path)
   - stdlib / native: the standard library or platform already does it; a
     new dependency for a few lines
   - yagni: abstraction with one implementation, config nobody sets
   - merge: near-copies that must change together
   - split: one function doing several unrelated jobs, so it is hard to read
     or test. Split by job, never by line count, and never into helpers that
     exist only to make a function shorter.

## 3. Check before you report

- Every finding needs a concrete case: "this input or situation leads to this
  wrong result". No case, no finding.
- Re-read the lines and confirm: the caller exists, the value can really be
  empty, the code really is unused.
- A shortcut marked with a `shortcut:` (or older `ponytail:`) comment that names its limit is a
  decision, not a finding, unless the expected load already crosses it.
- Propose the smallest fix that works. Prefer fixes that delete code. Never
  add layers, frameworks or config the problem does not need.
- No style taste, no "consider", no vague worries.

## 4. Output

Very simple English: short sentences, everyday words. Explain a technical
term the first time you use it. The reader may never have seen this code.

Start with `What this change does:` in two or three sentences.

Then the findings in three groups, skip empty groups:
- **Must fix:** bug, security, data loss, breaks at the expected load.
- **Should fix:** risky code without a test, real slowness, duplication, a
  function that mixes jobs, code that should not exist.
- **Nice to have:** small speed-ups, shorter forms.

Number findings across all groups, so the user can say "fix 2 and 5".
Every finding has all four parts, each one or two short sentences:

2. **Orders land on the wrong day** (`billing/close_day.py:L40-52`)
   - **What this is:** At midnight this job closes the day and bills all orders of that day.
   - **Problem:** It takes "today" from the server clock, which runs in UTC. An order placed
     at 00:30 in Berlin is billed on the day before.
   - **Fix:** Compute the day once in the shop's time zone:
     `datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin")).date()`. One line, nothing else changes.
   - **If we skip it:** Late orders show the wrong date, and accounting fixes them by hand.

End with:
- `Verdict: Ship.` or `Verdict: fix 1 and 3 first.`
- `Lean: -<N> lines possible.` when lean findings exist.
- `Not checked:` one line, if something mattered and you could not check it.

Nothing found: `What this change does:`, then `Looks good. Ship.` and one line
on what you checked.

Lists findings, changes no code.

```text
import { Migration } from "@medusajs/framework/mikro-orm/migrations"

export class Migration20260106185528 extends Migration {
  override async up(): Promise<void> {
    this.addSql(
      `alter table if exists "order_shipping_method_adjustment" add column if not exists "version" integer not null default 1;`
    )
    this.addSql(
      `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS "IDX_order_shipping_method_adjustment_version_shipping_method" ON "order_shipping_method_adjustment" ("version", "shipping_method_id") WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;`
    )
    this.addSql(`WITH latest_order_shipping_version AS (
          SELECT
            os.shipping_method_id AS shipping_method_id,
            MAX(os.version) AS version
          FROM "order_shipping" os
          WHERE os.deleted_at IS NULL
          GROUP BY os.shipping_method_id
        )
        UPDATE "order_shipping_method_adjustment" osma
        SET version = losv.version
        FROM latest_order_shipping_version losv
        WHERE osma.shipping_method_id = losv.shipping_method_id
          AND osma.version <> losv.version
        `)
  }

  override async down(): Promise<void> {
    this.addSql(
      `drop index if exists "IDX_order_shipping_method_adjustment_version_shipping_method";`
    )
    this.addSql(
      `alter table if exists "order_shipping_method_adjustment" drop column if exists "version";`
    )
  }
}
```

```text
import * as zod from "zod"

import { Button, Input, toast } from "@medusajs/ui"
import { RouteDrawer, useRouteModal } from "../../../../../../components/modals"

import { zodResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/zod"
import { AdminInventoryItem } from "@medusajs/types"
import { useForm } from "react-hook-form"
import { useTranslation } from "react-i18next"
import { z } from "zod"
import { Form } from "../../../../../../components/common/form"
import { KeyboundForm } from "../../../../../../components/utilities/keybound-form"
import { useUpdateInventoryItem } from "../../../../../../hooks/api/inventory"

type EditInventoryItemFormProps = {
  item: AdminInventoryItem
}

const EditInventoryItemSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().optional(),
  sku: z.string().min(1),
})

const getDefaultValues = (item: AdminInventoryItem) => {
  return {
    title: item.title ?? undefined,
    sku: item.sku ?? undefined,
  }
}

export const EditInventoryItemForm = ({ item }: EditInventoryItemFormProps) => {
  const { t } = useTranslation()
  const { handleSuccess } = useRouteModal()

  const form = useForm<zod.infer<typeof EditInventoryItemSchema>>({
    defaultValues: getDefaultValues(item),
    resolver: zodResolver(EditInventoryItemSchema),
  })

  const { mutateAsync, isPending: isLoading } = useUpdateInventoryItem(item.id)

  const handleSubmit = form.handleSubmit(async (values) => {
    mutateAsync(values as any, {
      onSuccess: () => {
        toast.success(t("inventory.toast.updateItem"))
        handleSuccess()
      },
      onError: (e) => toast.error(e.message),
    })
  })

  return (
    <RouteDrawer.Form form={form}>
      <KeyboundForm
        onSubmit={handleSubmit}
        className="flex flex-1 flex-col overflow-hidden"
      >
        <RouteDrawer.Body className="flex flex-1 flex-col gap-y-8 overflow-auto">
          <Form.Field
            control={form.control}
            name="title"
            render={({ field }) => {
              return (
                <Form.Item>
                  <Form.Label>{t("fields.title")}</Form.Label>
                  <Form.Control>
                    <Input {...field} />
                  </Form.Control>
                  <Form.ErrorMessage />
                </Form.Item>
              )
            }}
          />
          <Form.Field
            control={form.control}
            name="sku"
            render={({ field }) => {
              return (
                <Form.Item>
                  <Form.Label>{t("fields.sku")}</Form.Label>
                  <Form.Control>
                    <Input {...field} />
                  </Form.Control>
                  <Form.ErrorMessage />
                </Form.Item>
              )
            }}
          />
        </RouteDrawer.Body>
        <RouteDrawer.Footer>
          <div className="flex items-center justify-end gap-x-2">
            <RouteDrawer.Close asChild>
              <Button variant="secondary" size="small">
                {t("actions.cancel")}
              </Button>
            </RouteDrawer.Close>
            <Button type="submit" size="small" isLoading={isLoading}>
              {t("actions.save")}
            </Button>
          </div>
        </RouteDrawer.Footer>
      </KeyboundForm>
    </RouteDrawer.Form>
  )
}
```

```text
import schema from "../$schema.json"

const translationsDir = path.join(__dirname, "..")

function getRequiredKeysFromSchema(schema: any, prefix = ""): string[] {
  const keys: string[] = []

  if (schema.type === "object" && schema.properties) {
    Object.entries(schema.properties).forEach(([key, value]: [string, any]) => {
      const fullKey = prefix ? `${prefix}.${key}` : key

      if (value.type === "object") {
        keys.push(...getRequiredKeysFromSchema(value, fullKey))
      } else if (schema.required?.includes(key)) {
        keys.push(fullKey)
      }
    })
  }

  return keys.sort()
}

function getAllKeysFromSchema(schema: any, prefix = ""): Set<string> {
  const keys = new Set<string>()

  if (schema.type === "object" && schema.properties) {
    Object.entries(schema.properties).forEach(([key, value]: [string, any]) => {
      const fullKey = prefix ? `${prefix}.${key}` : key
      keys.add(fullKey)

      if (value.type === "object") {
        const nestedKeys = getAllKeysFromSchema(value, fullKey)
        nestedKeys.forEach((k) => keys.add(k))
      }
    })
  }

  return keys
}

function getTranslationKeys(obj: any, prefix = ""): string[] {
  const keys: string[] = []

  Object.entries(obj).forEach(([key, value]) => {
    const fullKey = prefix ? `${prefix}.${key}` : key

    if (value && typeof value === "object" && !Array.isArray(value)) {
      keys.push(...getTranslationKeys(value, fullKey))
    } else {
      keys.push(fullKey)
    }
  })

  return keys.sort()
}
```

```text
function findPluralGroups(
  obj: any,
  currentPath = ""
): Map<string, Set<string>> {
  const groups = new Map<string, Set<string>>()

  if (typeof obj !== "object" || obj === null || Array.isArray(obj)) {
    return groups
  }

  Object.entries(obj).forEach(([key, value]) => {
    const pluralMatch = key.match(/^(.+)_(zero|one|two|few|many|other)$/)

    if (pluralMatch) {
      const [, baseKey, form] = pluralMatch
      const fullPath = currentPath ? `${currentPath}.${baseKey}` : baseKey

      if (!groups.has(fullPath)) {
        groups.set(fullPath, new Set())
      }
      groups.get(fullPath)!.add(form)
    }

    if (value && typeof value === "object" && !Array.isArray(value)) {
      const fullPath = currentPath ? `${currentPath}.${key}` : key
      const nestedGroups = findPluralGroups(value, fullPath)
      nestedGroups.forEach((forms, path) => groups.set(path, forms))
    }
  })

  return groups
}
```

```typescript
    expect(getStockStatus(item(2, 3))).toBe("out_of_stock")
  })

  it("is out of stock when the item has no location levels", () => {
    expect(getStockStatus(item(null, null))).toBe("out_of_stock")
  })

  it("is out of stock at 0 even when the threshold is 0", () => {
    expect(getStockStatus(item(0, 0, 0))).toBe("out_of_stock")

  it("is low stock when available quantity equals the threshold", () => {
    expect(getStockStatus(item(12, 2, 10))).toBe("low_stock")
  })

  it("is low stock at 1 available", () => {
    expect(getStockStatus(item(1, 0, 10))).toBe("low_stock")
  })

  it("has no status when available quantity is above the threshold", () => {
    expect(getStockStatus(item(13, 2, 10))).toBeNull()
  })

  it("uses available, not stocked, quantity", () => {
    // 20 stocked is above 10, but 20 - 15 reserved = 5 is not
    expect(getStockStatus(item(20, 15, 10))).toBe("low_stock")

  it("never shows low stock when the threshold is 0", () => {
    expect(getStockStatus(item(1, 0, 0))).toBeNull()
  })

  it("respects a custom threshold", () => {
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-08 15:47:44Z)**_

Issue #61 is implemented on `feat/issue-61-configurable-low-stock-thresholds`, and all the tests I ran pass. Nothing is committed. I haven't opened the dashboard in a browser yet, so the edit drawer and badges are untested by hand.

**What changed**
- **Database:** inventory items have a new `low_stock_threshold` setting that defaults to 10. The migration (`Migration20261108153927.ts`) adds only this column. The migration generator also tried to change some unrelated columns, and I left those out.
- **Types:** the field is added to the inventory item types, and to the create and update inputs.
- **API:** create and update accept a whole number from 0 to 2,147,483,647, and inventory item responses now include the threshold.
  - Negative numbers, decimals, strings and null are rejected with a 400 error.
  - The upper limit is the largest number the database column can hold. Without it, a bigger number would pass and then crash the request.
- **Dashboard:**
  - The edit inventory item drawer has a threshold field. An empty field is rejected rather than saved as 0, because 0 would quietly turn the warning off.
  - The inventory list shows an orange "Low stock" badge or a red "Out of stock" badge, replacing the hardcoded badge from #18.
  - The status rule lives in one function, `getStockStatus`, so the tests check the real logic.
  - The labels are translatable, in the same sentence case as existing labels like "In stock".
- **Changeset:** `.changeset/inventory-low-stock-threshold.md`, matching how the team records each feature.

**Tests**
- **Dashboard unit tests:** I replaced the old test, which checked a copy of the logic instead of the real code. The new tests cover:
  - available stock at 0, below 0, and with no stock locations;
  - available stock equal to the threshold and one above it;
  - a threshold of 0;
  - a case where stocked quantity is above the threshold but available is not;
  - the badge each status shows.

  I broke the boundary on purpose to make sure the tests catch it, then put it back.
- **API integration tests:** the default of 10, a threshold of 0, the value persisting across a fetch and a list, the value surviving an unrelated update, and the five rejected inputs on both create and update.
- **Existing tests:** two reservations tests compare the full inventory item exactly, so I added the new field to their expected objects.

The PR description, test strategy and design decisions are saved in memory, ready for when you send the PR instructions.

- I didn't run the full integration test suite, only the suites listed above.
- I didn't test the migration against a database that already has inventory items. Postgres fills the new column with 10 for existing rows, and the test that fetches an earlier-created item supports that.

Review a change like the senior developer who will be paged when it breaks.
Order of importance: correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean.
Lean still matters: every extra line must be read, tested and fixed later.
This is a report the user asked for, so give it in full.

## 1. Understand first

- Review what the user names: uncommitted or staged changes, a branch, a PR
  link, or files. Nothing named: the uncommitted changes, or the last commit
  if there are none.
- Read the diff, then the code it touches: callers of every changed function,
  the functions it calls, the tests, the README.
- Trace the real flow: where data comes in, what is stored, what goes out.
- A change can break code it does not touch. When a signature, return value
  or behavior changes, grep every caller.
- Find the expected load in the repo (README, deploy config): one person
  running a script, or many users and processes at once. Judge scale against
  that, and say which load you assumed.

## 2. Look for

1. **Bug:** wrong result, crash, missed edge case (empty, zero, last item,
   rounding, time zones), a caller broken by the change, a fix applied in one
   caller while the shared function stays broken.
2. **Risk:** security holes (injection, weak randomness, secrets, missing
   checks on input from users), data loss (errors swallowed, writes in the
   wrong order, no transaction).
3. **Scale:** fine for one user, wrong for many: check-then-write races, the
   same work done by every process, memory or lists that only grow, a query
   per item, O(n^2) on big input, per-process state that must be shared.
4. **Missing test:** risky new logic (a branch, a parser, money, security,
   data writes, a bug fix) with no test that fails when it breaks. One good
   test, not coverage.
5. **Speed:** big slowdowns are problems. Small wins (work repeated in a hot
   loop) are suggestions; some software counts every millisecond.
6. **Lean:** code that should not exist or should be smaller.
   - delete: dead code, unused options, speculative features
   - reuse: the repo already has this helper (name the path)
   - stdlib / native: the standard library or platform already does it; a
     new dependency for a few lines
   - yagni: abstraction with one implementation, config nobody sets
   - merge: near-copies that must change together
   - split: one function doing several unrelated jobs, so it is hard to read
     or test. Split by job, never by line count, and never into helpers that
     exist only to make a function shorter.

## 3. Check before you report

- Every finding needs a concrete case: "this input or situation leads to this
  wrong result". No case, no finding.
- Re-read the lines and confirm: the caller exists, the value can really be
  empty, the code really is unused.
- A shortcut marked with a `shortcut:` (or older `ponytail:`) comment that names its limit is a
  decision, not a finding, unless the expected load already crosses it.
- Propose the smallest fix that works. Prefer fixes that delete code. Never
  add layers, frameworks or config the problem does not need.
- No style taste, no "consider", no vague worries.

## 4. Output

Very simple English: short sentences, everyday words. Explain a technical
term the first time you use it. The reader may never have seen this code.

Start with `What this change does:` in two or three sentences.

Then the findings in three groups, skip empty groups:
- **Must fix:** bug, security, data loss, breaks at the expected load.
- **Should fix:** risky code without a test, real slowness, duplication, a
  function that mixes jobs, code that should not exist.
- **Nice to have:** small speed-ups, shorter forms.

Number findings across all groups, so the user can say "fix 2 and 5".
Every finding has all four parts, each one or two short sentences:

2. **Orders land on the wrong day** (`billing/close_day.py:L40-52`)

   - **Problem:** It takes "today" from the server clock, which runs in UTC. An order placed
     at 00:30 in Berlin is billed on the day before.
   - **Fix:** Compute the day once in the shop's time zone:

   - **If we skip it:** Late orders show the wrong date, and accounting fixes them by hand.

End with:
- `Verdict: Ship.` or `Verdict: fix 1 and 3 first.`
- `Lean: -<N> lines possible.` when lean findings exist.
- `Not checked:` one line, if something mattered and you could not check it.

Nothing found: `What this change does:`, then `Looks good. Ship.` and one line

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-08 16:02:18Z)**_

The detail page asks for `*variants,...`. In Medusa, a field starting with `*` is added on top of the default fields rather than replacing them. The drawer fetches with the defaults, so the threshold is always loaded, which matches what you saw in the browser.

What this change does: it gives every inventory item a low-stock threshold, a number that defaults to 10 and is stored in a new database column. The admin API lets you set it, and the edit drawer has a field for it. The inventory list now shows a "Low stock" badge when available stock is above 0 and at or below the threshold, and an "Out of stock" badge when available stock is 0 or less. These badges replace the old hardcoded "under 10" badge.

I assumed admin-dashboard load: a few store staff editing items now and then. Nothing here adds queries or runs per request beyond simple arithmetic.

**Should fix**

1. **The empty-field rule in the edit form has no test** (`packages/admin/dashboard/src/routes/inventory/inventory-detail/components/edit-inventory-item/components/edit-item-form.tsx:L22-L25`)
   - **What this is:** The form's validation rule (its zod schema) turns the text in the threshold box into a number and rejects bad input.
   - **Problem:** It deliberately rejects an empty box, because otherwise clearing the box would quietly save 0 and switch the warning off. I only checked this with a one-off script, so nothing would catch it if someone later "simplifies" the rule to `z.coerce.number()`.
   - **Fix:** Export the schema and add one small test file that checks `""`, `" "`, `"-1"` and `"1.5"` are rejected and `"0"` is accepted. That's about 15 lines.
   - **If we skip it:** A future refactor could bring back the silent save of 0, and no test would fail.

**Nice to have**

2. **The database limit is copied in two validators** (`packages/medusa/src/api/admin/inventory-items/validators.ts:L130-L131, L155-L156`)
   - **What this is:** Create and update both say `z.number().int().min(0).max(2147483647)`, each with the same comment.
   - **Problem:** The two copies have to stay the same. If one changes and the other doesn't, create and update will accept different values.
   - **Fix:** Define it once in that file, for example `const LowStockThreshold = z.number().int().min(0).max(2147483647)` with the comment, and use it in both places. The dashboard form keeps its own copy, because the dashboard can't import from the server package.
   - **If we skip it:** Nothing breaks today. It's just one more place to keep in sync.

Verdict: Ship. Item 1 is worth doing before the PR because the PR template asks for tests on every behavior change.
Lean: -2 lines possible.
Not checked: whether the browser blocks a decimal like 1.5 with its own popup (because of `step={1}`) before the form shows its own error. Either way the value isn't saved.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-08 16:31:21Z)**_

Your browser's requests never reach the backend. Run from inside the container, the same two preflight checks are answered in about 10 ms. There are also zero open connections to port 9000 in the container, so the browser's requests are stuck before they get there. The problem is VS Code's port forwarding for 9000, not the code or the backend.

That forward most likely broke when the backend went down and restarted earlier (my server-package rebuild wiped the build output it was running from). The dashboard on 5173 loads because its forward is fine; only the one on 9000 is stuck.

To fix it:
1. In VS Code, open the **Ports** panel, next to the Terminal tab.
2. Right-click the row for **9000** and choose **Stop Forwarding Port**.
3. Click **Forward a Port** and enter `9000`.
4. Reload the dashboard.

If that doesn't help, run **Developer: Reload Window** from the command palette (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P). That re-creates all the port forwards and doesn't stop your dev servers.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.

Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## Before you write

Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.

## The smallest complete change

Take the first option that fully works:

1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.

- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.

Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.

## Levels

| Level | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.

Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## Before you write

Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.

## The smallest complete change

Take the first option that fully works:

1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.

- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.

Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.

## Levels

| Level | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |

````markdown
## Summary

**What** — What changes are introduced in this PR?

Inventory items get a configurable low-stock threshold, and the admin inventory list shows stock warnings based on it.

- New `low_stock_threshold` integer column on `inventory_item` (not null, default `10`), with a migration.
- `POST /admin/inventory-items` and `POST /admin/inventory-items/:id` accept `low_stock_threshold` (whole number, 0 to 2147483647). Inventory item responses include it by default.
- The edit inventory item drawer has a "Low stock threshold" field.
- The "In stock" column of the inventory list shows an orange **Low stock** badge when available quantity is above 0 and at or below the threshold, and a red **Out of stock** badge when it is 0 or less.
- This replaces the hardcoded "Low stock" text from #18 (stocked quantity below 10).

**Why** — Why are these changes relevant or necessary?

Closes #61

Store managers need to see which items to restock before they sell out, and a fixed cutoff of 10 does not fit every product.

**How** — How have these changes been implemented?

- **Model and migration:** `low_stock_threshold: model.number().default(10)` on `InventoryItem`. The migration adds the column with `default 10`, so existing rows get 10. The module snapshot has the new column.
- **Types:** the field is added to `InventoryItemDTO`, `CreateInventoryItemInput` (update extends it), `AdminInventoryItem` and `AdminCreateInventoryItem` (update extends it).
- **API:** one shared `LowStockThreshold` zod rule (`int`, `min(0)`, `max(2147483647)`) in both validators. The field is added to `defaultAdminInventoryItemFields`. The existing create and update workflows pass it through unchanged.
- **Dashboard:**
  - `getStockStatus()` in `use-inventory-table-columns.tsx` works out available quantity (total stocked minus total reserved) and returns `out_of_stock`, `low_stock` or nothing. The column renders it with `StatusBadge`.
  - The edit form schema moved to `edit-inventory-item/schema.ts`. It rejects an empty field instead of saving it as 0.
  - Four i18n keys are added to `en.json`, and `$schema.json` was regenerated.
- A changeset is included (patch).

**Testing** — How have these changes been tested, or how can the reviewer test the feature?

See **Test Evidence** below.

To try it locally:
1. Run `npx medusa db:migrate` in your backend.
2. Open Inventory, open an item, choose Edit and set the threshold.
3. Change the stock levels and check the badge in the list.

---

## Examples

```ts
// Set the threshold for an item (admin API / JS SDK)
await sdk.admin.inventoryItem.update("iitem_123", { low_stock_threshold: 5 })

// Rejected with 400: negative, decimal, null, string, or above 2147483647
await sdk.admin.inventoryItem.update("iitem_123", { low_stock_threshold: -1 })

// Dashboard status rule
getStockStatus({ stocked_quantity: 20, reserved_quantity: 15, low_stock_threshold: 10 })
// => "low_stock" (available is 5)
```

---

## Design

**Decision:** The threshold is stored once per inventory item, not per inventory item at each stock location.

**Alternatives considered:**
- One threshold per inventory item (a column on `inventory_item`).
- One threshold per location level (a column on `inventory_level`).
- Store it in the item's `metadata` JSON instead of a real column.

**Rationale:**
- The inventory list shows one row per item, with quantities summed across locations. A per-item threshold compares against the number the manager actually sees.
- Per-location would need a different UI, on the location levels table of the detail page.
- `metadata` cannot be validated as a non-negative integer at the API, and it has no default.

**Consequences:**
- Easier: one column, one form field, and the warning lines up with the list's numbers.
- Harder: an item that is low at one warehouse but fine overall shows no warning. Per-location thresholds would need a new column and UI later.

**Decision:** Items without a set threshold use 10, stored as a column default.

**Alternatives considered:**
- Column `default(10)`, not nullable. The migration fills existing rows.
- A nullable column, with null treated as 10 in the dashboard.
- A nullable column, with null meaning no low-stock warning.

**Rationale:**
- 10 keeps the behavior managers already had from #18.
- A stored default means the edit form always shows a real number, and no code needs a "null means 10" special case.
- A manager can still turn the warning off by setting 0.

**Consequences:**
- Easier: a simple required integer everywhere (API, types, form).
- Harder: there is no "unset" state, so changing the default later means a migration, not a code change.

**Other decisions:**
- **Available quantity:** total stocked minus total reserved across all locations. Incoming quantity is not counted.
- **No location levels:** an item with no location levels counts as **Out of stock**.
- **Threshold 0:** setting 0 turns off the low-stock warning. "Out of stock" still shows.
- **Status computed in the dashboard:** there is no API filter or sort by status. That was agreed as out of scope.
- **Open question on items that don't track stock:** handled by nothing. `manage_inventory` is a product variant setting, and inventory items always track stock.
- **Label case:** labels use sentence case ("Low stock", "Out of stock") to match existing dashboard labels like "In stock".

---

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- The Postgres integer limit `2147483647` appears in both the API validator and the dashboard form schema, because the dashboard cannot import server code. If the column type changes, both must change.
- The stock status is worked out only in the dashboard. A future status filter, or the alerts dashboard from the separate issue, would have to move or copy this rule to the server.

**Encountered:**
- `yarn migration:create` in the inventory module also generated unrelated `ALTER`s on the `inventory_level.raw_*` columns, plus formatting changes across the whole snapshot file. I kept only the `low_stock_threshold` change in both. The unrelated drift is left for a separate fix.
- The #18 badge test (`use-inventory-table-columns.spec.tsx`) tested a copy of the logic written inside the test, not the real column, so it could not fail. It is replaced with tests of `getStockStatus` and of the rendered column.
- `packages/core/types/src/http/inventory/admin/payloads.ts` already failed Prettier on `develop` (the `AdminUpdateInventoryItem` line). Left as is.

---

## Test Evidence

| Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
|---|---|---|---|
| AC1: Managers can configure and update a non-negative integer threshold through the admin interface | `inventory.spec.ts` › low_stock_threshold › should create an inventory item with a threshold of 0; › should persist an updated threshold and return it when listing; › should reject a negative / a decimal / a too large / a null / a string threshold on create and update. `schema.spec.ts` › rejects "", " ", "-1", "1.5", "abc", "2147483648"; › accepts "0", "25", 10. Manual: TODO(you) | integration, unit, manual | AC (non-negative integer). Upper limit: Postgres docs (integer range) |
| AC2: Threshold values persist and are unchanged after refresh | `inventory.spec.ts` › should persist an updated threshold and return it when listing; › should keep the threshold when other fields are updated; › should default to 10 when no threshold is given. Manual: TODO(you) | integration, manual | AC. Default 10: issue discussion |
| AC3: "Low stock" shows when available is > 0 and <= threshold | `use-inventory-table-columns.spec.tsx` › getStockStatus › is low stock when available quantity equals the threshold; › is low stock at 1 available; › uses available, not stocked, quantity; › respects a custom threshold. › In stock column › shows the low stock badge | unit | AC |
| AC4: Available quantity of 0 or less is "Out of stock", whatever the threshold | getStockStatus › is out of stock when available quantity is 0; › is out of stock when available quantity is negative; › is out of stock at 0 even when the threshold is 0; › is out of stock when the item has no location levels. › In stock column › shows the out of stock badge | unit | AC. No location levels: issue discussion |
| AC5: No warning above the threshold | getStockStatus › has no status when available quantity is above the threshold; › never shows low stock when the threshold is 0; › respects a custom threshold. › In stock column › shows no badge above the threshold | unit | AC |
| AC6: Existing inventory functionality keeps working | All existing tests in `inventory.spec.ts` (39 total pass), `inventory-import.spec.ts`, `reservations.spec.ts`, the inventory module integration tests, and 26 other HTTP suites plus 11 module suites that use inventory items (see results below) | integration | Existing tests (upstream behavior) |
| AC7: Automated tests cover validation, persistence and classification | Rows AC1 to AC5 | unit, integration | AC |
````

## Summary

**What** — What changes are introduced in this PR?

Inventory items get a configurable low-stock threshold, and the admin inventory list shows stock warnings based on it.

- New `low_stock_threshold` integer column on `inventory_item` (not null, default `10`), with a migration.
- `POST /admin/inventory-items` and `POST /admin/inventory-items/:id` accept `low_stock_threshold` (whole number, 0 to 2147483647). Inventory item responses include it by default.
- The edit inventory item drawer has a "Low stock threshold" field.
- The "In stock" column of the inventory list shows an orange **Low stock** badge when available quantity is above 0 and at or below the threshold, and a red **Out of stock** badge when it is 0 or less.
- This replaces the hardcoded "Low stock" text from #18 (stocked quantity below 10).

**Why** — Why are these changes relevant or necessary?

Closes #61

Store managers need to see which items to restock before they sell out, and a fixed cutoff of 10 does not fit every product.

**How** — How have these changes been implemented?

- **Model and migration:** `low_stock_threshold: model.number().default(10)` on `InventoryItem`. The migration adds the column with `default 10`, so existing rows get 10. The module snapshot has the new column.
- **Types:** the field is added to `InventoryItemDTO`, `CreateInventoryItemInput` (update extends it), `AdminInventoryItem` and `AdminCreateInventoryItem` (update extends it).
- **API:** one shared `LowStockThreshold` zod rule (`int`, `min(0)`, `max(2147483647)`) in both validators. The field is added to `defaultAdminInventoryItemFields`. The existing create and update workflows pass it through unchanged.
- **Dashboard:**
  - `getStockStatus()` in `use-inventory-table-columns.tsx` works out available quantity (total stocked minus total reserved) and returns `out_of_stock`, `low_stock` or nothing. The column renders it with `StatusBadge`.
  - The edit form schema moved to `edit-inventory-item/schema.ts`. It rejects an empty field instead of saving it as 0.
  - Four i18n keys are added to `en.json`, and `$schema.json` was regenerated.
- A changeset is included (patch).

**Testing** — How have these changes been tested, or how can the reviewer test the feature?

See **Test Evidence** below.

To try it locally:
1. Run `npx medusa db:migrate` in your backend.
2. Open Inventory, open an item, choose Edit and set the threshold.
3. Change the stock levels and check the badge in the list.

---

## Examples

```ts
// Set the threshold for an item (admin API / JS SDK)
await sdk.admin.inventoryItem.update("iitem_123", { low_stock_threshold: 5 })

// Rejected with 400: negative, decimal, null, string, or above 2147483647
await sdk.admin.inventoryItem.update("iitem_123", { low_stock_threshold: -1 })

// Dashboard status rule
getStockStatus({ stocked_quantity: 20, reserved_quantity: 15, low_stock_threshold: 10 })
// => "low_stock" (available is 5)
```

---

## Design

**Decision:** The threshold is stored once per inventory item, not per inventory item at each stock location.

**Alternatives considered:**
- One threshold per inventory item (a column on `inventory_item`).
- One threshold per location level (a column on `inventory_level`).
- Store it in the item's `metadata` JSON instead of a real column.

**Rationale:**
- The inventory list shows one row per item, with quantities summed across locations. A per-item threshold compares against the number the manager actually sees.
- Per-location would need a different UI, on the location levels table of the detail page.
- `metadata` cannot be validated as a non-negative integer at the API, and it has no default.

**Consequences:**
- Easier: one column, one form field, and the warning lines up with the list's numbers.
- Harder: an item that is low at one warehouse but fine overall shows no warning. Per-location thresholds would need a new column and UI later.

**Decision:** Items without a set threshold use 10, stored as a column default.

**Alternatives considered:**
- Column `default(10)`, not nullable. The migration fills existing rows.
- A nullable column, with null treated as 10 in the dashboard.
- A nullable column, with null meaning no low-stock warning.

**Rationale:**
- 10 keeps the behavior managers already had from #18.
- A stored default means the edit form always shows a real number, and no code needs a "null means 10" special case.
- A manager can still turn the warning off by setting 0.

**Consequences:**
- Easier: a simple required integer everywhere (API, types, form).
- Harder: there is no "unset" state, so changing the default later means a migration, not a code change.

**Other decisions:**
- **Available quantity:** total stocked minus total reserved across all locations. Incoming quantity is not counted.
- **No location levels:** an item with no location levels counts as **Out of stock**.
- **Threshold 0:** setting 0 turns off the low-stock warning. "Out of stock" still shows.
- **Status computed in the dashboard:** there is no API filter or sort by status. That was agreed as out of scope.
- **Open question on items that don't track stock:** handled by nothing. `manage_inventory` is a product variant setting, and inventory items always track stock.
- **Label case:** labels use sentence case ("Low stock", "Out of stock") to match existing dashboard labels like "In stock".

---

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- The Postgres integer limit `2147483647` appears in both the API validator and the dashboard form schema, because the dashboard cannot import server code. If the column type changes, both must change.
- The stock status is worked out only in the dashboard. A future status filter, or the alerts dashboard from the separate issue, would have to move or copy this rule to the server.

**Encountered:**
- `yarn migration:create` in the inventory module also generated unrelated `ALTER`s on the `inventory_level.raw_*` columns, plus formatting changes across the whole snapshot file. I kept only the `low_stock_threshold` change in both. The unrelated drift is left for a separate fix.
- The #18 badge test (`use-inventory-table-columns.spec.tsx`) tested a copy of the logic written inside the test, not the real column, so it could not fail. It is replaced with tests of `getStockStatus` and of the rendered column.
- `packages/core/types/src/http/inventory/admin/payloads.ts` already failed Prettier on `develop` (the `AdminUpdateInventoryItem` line). Left as is.
